text: Last year the regional grocery chain Fernway replaced the self-checkout kiosks in its twelve largest stores with staffed checkout lanes. In the following six months, average weekly sales in those twelve stores rose by 9 percent, while sales in Fernway's other stores, which kept their kiosks, were essentially flat. Fernway's management concludes that shoppers prefer staffed lanes and that converting the remaining stores would raise sales there by a similar amount.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens management's conclusion?
options: Staffed checkout lanes cost Fernway more to operate per transaction than self-checkout kiosks do.
Several of Fernway's smaller stores are located in towns where no competing grocery store operates.
During the same six months, a rival chain closed stores near nine of the twelve converted Fernway stores but near none of Fernway's other stores.
Some shoppers at the converted stores have asked Fernway to bring back at least a few self-checkout kiosks.
Fernway's twelve largest stores had higher average weekly sales than its other stores even before the conversion, and they also carry a much wider range of fresh and prepared foods.
explanation: The argument credits the staffed lanes for the 9 percent rise. If a competitor closed stores near most of the converted locations, its former customers offer an alternative cause for the jump, and that cause would not repeat at the other stores. Choice (A) concerns costs, not whether sales rise. Choice (E) is tempting, but a higher starting level does not explain why sales grew only in the converted stores.

text: To reduce traffic deaths, the city of Marlow lowered the speed limit on its residential streets from 40 to 30 kilometers per hour. Critics argue that drivers simply ignore posted limits, so the change will have no effect. City planners respond that even a small drop in average speed sharply reduces the chance that a pedestrian struck by a car is killed, and they predict that pedestrian deaths on residential streets will fall.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the planners' prediction?
options: Measurements taken in other cities after similar changes found that average speeds on residential streets fell by several kilometers per hour even though many drivers still exceeded the new limit.

Most traffic deaths in Marlow occur on highways and major roads rather than on residential streets, so the new limit, which does not cover those roads, addresses only a minority of the city's traffic deaths.
Marlow's residents were surveyed and a majority said they supported the lower speed limit.
Drivers who ignore speed limits are also more likely than other drivers to ignore stop signs.
The cost of replacing the speed limit signs on Marlow's residential streets was paid from the city's road maintenance budget.
explanation: The planners need average speeds to drop at least a little, despite the critics' claim that drivers ignore the limit. Evidence that average speeds fell elsewhere even while many drivers broke the limit answers the critics directly. Choice (C) shows support for the policy, but approval does not show that anyone drives more slowly. Choice (B) suggests the policy targets a small share of deaths, which does not support the prediction.

text: In a two-year field study, researchers studying a population of desert lizards in southern Morocco found that individuals with darker skin spent, on average, 20 minutes less each morning basking in the sun before beginning to forage than lighter-skinned individuals did. Because darker skin absorbs heat faster, the researchers concluded that dark coloration gives these lizards an advantage: more time each day for finding food.

stem: The researchers' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Lighter-skinned lizards are more common in the population than darker-skinned lizards.
Darker-skinned lizards are more easily seen by predators than lighter-skinned lizards are, especially on the pale sand where most of the population's foraging takes place.
Basking in the sun is the only way these lizards can raise their body temperature.
The lizards studied belong to a species that has been observed in several different deserts.
Darker-skinned lizards do not have to stop foraging correspondingly earlier in the day, for instance because they overheat sooner.
explanation: The conclusion is that darker lizards gain foraging time. That follows only if the 20 minutes saved in the morning is not lost later, for example by having to retreat from the heat sooner. If darker lizards overheat earlier and stop foraging earlier, the advantage disappears, so the argument assumes this does not happen. Choice (B) would point to a cost of dark skin, but the conclusion concerns only foraging time, so the argument does not need to rule it out.

text: A large national health survey, repeated every year, found that the share of adults who reported getting at least the recommended amount of weekly exercise rose from 41 percent to 48 percent over a decade. During the same decade, however, the share of adults classified as obese also rose, and average daily calorie intake per person, as measured by food purchase records, changed very little.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Obesity rates rose faster among adults over sixty than among younger adults.
Over the decade, people became more likely to overstate how much they exercise when answering survey questions, because exercise had become more widely seen as a social virtue.
Many adults who exercise regularly also try to limit the amount of sugar they eat.
The survey was conducted by telephone at the start of the decade and online at the end, and the online version asked about exercise using somewhat different wording.
Food purchase records do not capture food eaten in restaurants.
explanation: The puzzle is that exercise apparently rose while obesity also rose and calorie intake held steady. If the rise in reported exercise reflects growing overstatement rather than real activity, actual exercise may not have increased, and rising obesity is no longer surprising. Choice (E) questions the calorie data, but nothing suggests restaurant eating changed over the decade, so it does not explain the trend. Choice (D) notes a method change without saying how it would bias the results.

text: Historians have long held that the medieval town of Veldt declined because a new trade route bypassed it. ⟦Yet tax records show that Veldt's population began to fall two decades before the new route opened.⟧ This timing does not by itself refute the trade-route account, since merchants may have anticipated the route and moved early. But letters from Veldt's council in those years complain repeatedly of flooding and say nothing about trade. ⟦The best explanation, then, is that the decline began with environmental damage and was only later accelerated by the change in trade.⟧

stem: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered in support of that conclusion.
The first is a claim the argument rejects; the second is the position the argument defends.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support a rival account; the second is that rival account, which the argument goes on to accept only in part.
The first is evidence that casts doubt on a traditional account; the second is the argument's main conclusion, which revises that account.
The first is a consideration the argument concedes is decisive; the second is an objection to that consideration.
explanation: The first portion, the early population decline, is evidence that challenges the historians' trade-route view. The argument then concedes this evidence is not decisive, adds the council letters, and concludes with the second portion, which keeps trade as a later factor but puts environmental damage first. Choice (B) is tempting, but the argument never rejects the tax-record evidence; it relies on it. Choice (E) fails because the argument says the timing is not decisive.

text: A furniture factory installed a camera system that inspects every glued joint on its chairs and tables before they are packed. In the year after the system was installed, the number of products returned by customers because of loose or broken joints fell by 30 percent. The factory's production director concludes that the cameras were responsible for most of this reduction and recommends buying a more advanced version of the system.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the director's conclusion?
options: In the same year, the factory introduced far fewer new furniture designs than usual, and in earlier years most joint failures had occurred in newly introduced designs.
The more advanced version of the camera system costs roughly three times as much as the version the factory now uses.
Some workers at the factory disliked the system at first because it flagged many sound joints as faulty, which slowed production and led a few teams to switch it off for several weeks.
Customers returned products through the same online form and under the same return policy both before and after the system was installed.
Other furniture makers that installed similar camera systems have generally continued to use them for several years afterward.
explanation: The director attributes the drop in returns to the cameras. If the factory introduced far fewer new designs that year, and new designs are where most joint failures arise, there were simply fewer weak points to fail, which explains the drop without the cameras. Choice (B) bears on whether to buy the upgrade but not on what caused the reduction. Choice (D) rules out one alternative explanation, a change in how returns were made, so it slightly supports the director.

text: At Corlan Furniture, every product sold online is also sold in at least one of the company's showrooms. Some products sold in showrooms are made to order and take more than eight weeks to deliver. No product that takes more than eight weeks to deliver is eligible for the company's free-return guarantee. All products sold online, however, are eligible for the free-return guarantee.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Every product sold in Corlan's showrooms is also sold online.
Some products sold online are made to order.
Most of Corlan's showroom products are eligible for the free-return guarantee.
Some products sold in Corlan's showrooms are not sold online.
No made-to-order product at Corlan can be delivered in less than eight weeks, whether it is bought in a showroom or online.
explanation: Some showroom products take more than eight weeks, so those products are not eligible for the guarantee. Every online product is eligible, so those slow showroom products cannot be sold online; therefore some showroom products are not sold online. Choice (A) contradicts this. Choice (B) is the reverse of what follows: nothing says online products are made to order, and the slow made-to-order items are excluded from online sales. Choice (E) goes beyond the statements, which say only that some made-to-order products take more than eight weeks.

text: The province of Tessaly plans to give a tax credit to farmers who plant strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields. Supporters say the strips will attract wild bees and other pollinators, and that higher pollinator numbers will raise the yields of nearby crops such as apples and canola enough to more than repay farmers for the land the strips take out of production.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the supporters' claim?
options: Whether the wildflower species proposed for the strips are native to Tessaly
Whether farmers in Tessaly have received tax credits for other conservation practices in the past
Whether the yields of apples and canola in Tessaly are currently limited by a shortage of pollinators
Whether wildflower strips are more attractive to look at than the grass borders they would replace
Whether the tax credit would cost the province more than it collects each year from taxes on farmland in the regions where most apples and canola are grown
explanation: The claim is that more pollinators will raise yields enough to repay the lost land. That chain works only if yields are now held back by too few pollinators; if crops are already fully pollinated, extra bees add nothing. Choice (E) concerns the cost to the province, not whether farmers' gains exceed their losses. Choice (A) might matter for ecology, but the claim does not depend on whether the flowers are native.

text: A study followed 3,000 call-center employees at large firms for five years, checking in with each of them every six months. Those who used standing desks for at least half of their working day reported back pain far less often than those who sat all day. The study's authors conclude that standing for part of the day prevents back pain and recommend that employers provide standing desks to all of their staff.

stem: Which of the following, if true, casts the most doubt on the authors' conclusion?
options: Standing desks are more expensive than ordinary desks, though their prices have fallen in recent years.
Workers who stood for most of the day were about as likely to report foot pain as those who sat all day.

Some of the workers who sat all day exercised regularly outside of work, and most of these regular exercisers reported little or no back pain at any of the check-ins during the five years of the study.
The study included workers in several countries, and the rates of back pain differed somewhat from one country to another.
Workers who already had back problems at the start of the study were much more likely than other workers to avoid standing desks because standing aggravated their pain.
explanation: The authors infer that standing prevents back pain from the fact that standers reported less of it. If people with existing back trouble chose not to stand, the sitters' group started out with more back pain, so the difference may reflect who chose each desk rather than any effect of standing. Choice (C) shows that some sitters avoided back pain, but that is compatible with standing still helping on average. Choice (A) concerns the recommendation's cost, not the causal claim.

text: A science journalist, writing about a large survey of how often published papers are cited, argues: "Research papers whose findings are later contradicted by other studies receive, on average, more citations than papers whose findings hold up. Clearly, then, scientists are more interested in sensational claims than in reliable ones, and the citation system, which shapes hiring and funding decisions, rewards bad science."

stem: The journalist's reasoning is most vulnerable to which of the following criticisms?
options: It relies on the opinions of journalists rather than on the views of practicing scientists.
It overlooks the possibility that many of the citations a contradicted paper receives come from the very studies that test and dispute its findings.
It assumes that a paper whose findings are contradicted must have been dishonestly produced.
It treats the number of citations a paper receives as though it were a precise measure of the paper's scientific quality, rather than one rough indicator among several.
It fails to consider that some fields of science produce many more papers each year than other fields do.
explanation: The journalist takes high citation counts as a sign that scientists favor sensational claims. But checking and disputing a finding also requires citing it, so a contradicted paper may gather citations precisely because others challenged it, which is not a reward. Choice (D) is tempting, yet the journalist's point is about what citations reveal about interest, not a claim that they measure quality precisely. Choice (C) misdescribes the argument, which never mentions dishonesty.

text: Three years ago the port city of Halvik began requiring cruise ships docked in its harbor during the summer season to plug into the city's electricity supply instead of running their diesel engines. Since then, air-quality monitors in the harbor district record a 15 percent drop in summer fine-particle pollution. The port authority concludes that the rule is the main reason for the improvement and argues that applying the same rule to cruise ships docked in winter would produce a comparable improvement in winter air.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the authority's argument that a winter rule would produce a comparable improvement?
options: Before the rule was introduced, summer pollution in the harbor district was worse than pollution anywhere else in Halvik.
Fees paid by ships for the city's electricity have been used to buy cleaner ferries that serve the harbor all year round.
Some cruise lines that formerly docked in Halvik in summer now schedule more of their visits for the winter months, when the rule does not apply, so winter cruise visits have risen noticeably.
Few cruise ships dock in Halvik in winter, and most of the harbor district's winter fine-particle pollution comes from wood-burning stoves in its older apartment buildings.
Fine-particle pollution in nearby ports that have no such rule has stayed roughly constant over the past three years.
explanation: The argument predicts that the same rule would bring the same benefit in winter, which assumes that winter pollution, like summer pollution, comes largely from docked cruise ships. If few ships dock in winter and wood stoves produce most winter particles, the rule would touch little of the problem. Choice (C) is the attractive trap: more winter visits mean more winter ship pollution, which if anything gives a winter rule more to remove, so it does not undercut the prediction. Choice (B) offers another cause of improvement, but the ferries run all year, so they do not explain a summer-only effect.

text: Ashcombe, a maker of kitchen appliances, reviewed ten years of sales data and found that customers who registered their products online were twice as likely as other customers to buy a second Ashcombe product within two years. Ashcombe's marketing director therefore proposes offering a small gift card to every customer who registers, reasoning that a higher registration rate will bring a corresponding increase in repeat purchases.

stem: The marketing director's reasoning relies on which of the following assumptions?
options: The cost of the gift cards, together with the cost of handling the extra registrations, will be lower than the profit Ashcombe earns on the additional repeat purchases.
Registering a product, rather than some prior attachment to the brand that also makes customers likely to register, is at least partly what makes those customers more likely to buy again.
Customers who receive a gift card will be more likely than other customers to spend the card on a Ashcombe product.
Most customers who do not now register their products are unaware that registration is possible, even though instructions are printed on every box.
Ashcombe's competitors do not already offer gift cards or other rewards to customers who register their products.
explanation: The director moves from a correlation (registrants buy again more often) to a prediction that inducing more registrations will raise repeat buying. That works only if registration itself, for example through follow-up offers, contributes to repeat buying, rather than both simply reflecting existing loyalty. Choice (A) is tempting, but the reasoning concludes only that repeat purchases will increase, not that the plan is profitable. Choice (D) offers one reason people fail to register, but the plan could work whatever the reason.

text: When Harwick University replaced the lighting in its classroom buildings with LED lamps, which use about half as much electricity to produce the same amount of light, administrators expected the electricity bill for lighting those buildings to fall substantially. Two years after the replacement was completed, however, the bill was only slightly lower than before, even though electricity prices had not risen and the buildings had not been enlarged.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the lighting bill did not fall as much as administrators expected?
options: LED lamps last several times longer than the lamps they replaced, which has reduced the university's spending on maintenance staff.
Some instructors complained that the light from the new lamps appeared harsher and bluer than the old light, and the university responded by fitting diffusing covers to the lamps in many classrooms.
Several other universities that installed LED lighting in the same years reported much larger savings than Harwick did.
Lighting accounts for only a small part of the university's total electricity consumption.
Because the new lamps were cheap to run, the university installed more of them than before and kept corridors and study rooms lit through the night.
explanation: The expectation assumed the university would buy the same amount of light at half the power. If it instead installed more lamps and kept many lit all night, it used much of the efficiency gain to produce more light, so total consumption fell only a little. Choice (A) concerns maintenance, not the electricity bill. Choice (C) deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it, and (D) concerns total use, while the bill in question is for lighting alone.

text: Historians have generally attributed the rapid spread of printing workshops in sixteenth-century Brabant to the growing wealth of the region's merchants, who bought books in large numbers. One historian argues instead that the decisive factor was the founding of several universities in the region, whose students and teachers created a steady demand for printed textbooks, and that merchant wealth mattered much less than has been claimed.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the historian's argument?
options: Surviving inventories show that workshops opened mainly in university towns, including some with few wealthy merchants, but not in rich trading towns lacking a university.
Wealthy merchants in sixteenth-century Brabant often owned private libraries that included books printed in other regions.
Universities in sixteenth-century Brabant required students to buy their own copies of assigned texts, and many students could not afford the copies sold by booksellers from other regions.
The number of printing workshops in neighboring regions also increased during the sixteenth century.
Some printers in Brabant produced both textbooks and decorative books intended for wealthy households.
explanation: The historian's claim is comparative: universities, not merchant wealth, drove the spread. Evidence that workshops followed universities even where merchants were few, and failed to appear in rich towns without universities, separates the two factors and favors the historian. Choice (C) is tempting because it explains why universities created demand, but it does nothing to show that merchant wealth mattered less. Choice (B) suggests merchants also bought books from elsewhere, which only weakly bears on local workshops.

text: Some ecologists have proposed releasing a parasitic wasp to control the beetle that is killing ash trees in Lindor Forest. ⟦In laboratory trials, the wasp killed nearly all of the beetle larvae it was given.⟧ Opponents warn that the wasp might also attack native beetles. That risk appears small, since the wasp in trials ignored every native species offered to it. But laboratory success does not guarantee success outdoors: ⟦the beetle larvae in Lindor Forest live deep under thick bark, where the wasp, whose egg-laying organ is short, may be unable to reach most of them.⟧ The release should therefore be preceded by a field trial.

stem: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is a consideration that the argument rejects.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its conclusion; the second is a qualification of that conclusion.
The first is evidence offered in support of a proposal; the second is a consideration that the argument uses to show that this evidence does not settle whether the proposal would work.
The first is a finding that opponents of the proposal use against it; the second is evidence that the argument offers in support of the proposal.
The first is a claim that the argument disputes; the second is evidence that the argument cites in support of the opponents' warning that the wasp might also attack the forest's native beetles.
explanation: The first portion is the laboratory evidence behind the proposal to release the wasp. The second portion explains why that evidence may not carry over to the forest, which supports the actual conclusion that a field trial should come first. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: the second portion raises a doubt, but about reaching the target beetles, not about harm to native species, which the argument judges a small risk. Choice (B) fails because the conclusion is the call for a field trial, and the first portion does not support that call directly.

text: In a clinical trial, patients recovering from knee surgery were randomly assigned either to a standard physical therapy program or to the same program plus daily sessions with a new motion-tracking app that gives feedback on exercise form. After twelve weeks, the app group had regained significantly more range of motion. The app's developer concludes that the feedback on form is what produced the better recovery.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the developer's conclusion?
options: Patients in the app group were, on average, slightly younger than patients in the standard group, although the difference was not statistically significant.
Records from the app show that patients in the app group completed far more exercise repetitions each week than patients in the standard group did.
The motion-tracking app is considerably more expensive than a standard course of physical therapy, so many insurers may decline to pay for it.
Some patients in the app group reported that the app's feedback was occasionally inaccurate when they exercised in poorly lit rooms.
Range of motion is only one of several measures that physical therapists use to judge how well a patient is recovering from knee surgery.
explanation: Random assignment makes the groups comparable, so the app probably did cause better recovery; the question is which feature of it did. If app users simply exercised much more, the extra practice, perhaps prompted by reminders, could explain the gains without any help from feedback on form. Choice (A) is the attractive trap, but the age difference is small and not significant, which randomization is expected to produce. Choices (C) and (E) concern cost and how recovery is measured, not the cause of the measured improvement.

text: A survey of a coral reef found that every colony of the coral species Acropora velata that had bleached during the previous summer's heat wave was located in water shallower than four meters. Not every colony in water shallower than four meters bleached, however. All colonies of the species that host the alga strain Type D, which is known to tolerate heat, were found in water deeper than four meters.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true of Acropora velata colonies on the reef?
options: Every colony that did not bleach hosts the alga strain Type D.
Colonies in water shallower than four meters bleach because they lack the alga strain Type D.
Most colonies in water deeper than four meters host the alga strain Type D.
Some colonies in water deeper than four meters bleached during the heat wave.
None of the colonies hosting the alga strain Type D bleached.
explanation: Every bleached colony was in shallow water, and every Type D colony was in deep water, so no Type D colony can have been among the bleached ones. Choice (B) is tempting because Type D is heat-tolerant, but the statements establish only where colonies are, not why they bleached; that causal claim does not follow. Choice (A) fails because shallow colonies that did not bleach cannot host Type D, and (D) contradicts the first statement.

text: Over the past five years, the share of new cars sold in the country of Vellmark that are electric has risen from 4 percent to 31 percent, and the number of public charging stations has more than quadrupled. Yet over the same period, the average revenue that a Vellmark gas station earns from selling fuel has fallen by only about 3 percent, while total spending on fuel nationwide has fallen far more.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy above?
options: Over the five years, hundreds of small gas stations closed, and many of their former customers now buy fuel at the gas stations that remain.
Electric cars in Vellmark are driven, on average, slightly fewer kilometers per year than gasoline cars are.
The price of fuel in Vellmark rose sharply during the first two of the five years and then fell back to about its original level.
Many of Vellmark's gas stations now earn a growing share of their income from selling snacks, coffee, and car-washing services rather than from selling fuel.
Because most cars remain in use for well over a decade, electric cars still make up only a small share of all the cars on Vellmark's roads.
explanation: The puzzle is that national fuel spending fell far more than the average station's fuel revenue. If many stations closed and their customers moved to the survivors, the national total could fall sharply while the shrinking number of stations each kept nearly the same revenue. Choice (E) is the trap; it explains why fuel spending has not collapsed, but it applies equally to the national total and so cannot explain the gap between the two figures. Choice (D) concerns non-fuel income, which is outside the revenue being compared.

text: To reduce evictions, the city of Rosendal plans to give tenants who receive an eviction notice free access to a lawyer. Officials note that, in the city's housing court, tenants who had a lawyer were evicted less than half as often as tenants who represented themselves. They conclude that providing lawyers to all tenants facing eviction will substantially reduce evictions in the city.

stem: The officials' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most tenants who receive an eviction notice in Rosendal cannot afford to hire a lawyer at current market rates.
The program will not cost the city more than it currently spends on emergency shelter for evicted households.
Landlords in Rosendal will not respond to the program by raising rents for all tenants.
The tenants who hired lawyers in the past did not, for the most part, have stronger cases than tenants who represented themselves.
Tenants who represent themselves in housing court are usually unfamiliar with the court's rules and procedures.
explanation: The officials infer from past outcomes that lawyers cause lower eviction rates. If the tenants who hired lawyers had mostly stronger cases, for example because lawyers took only winnable ones, the lower rate reflects case strength, and giving lawyers to everyone would help much less. The argument must assume this was not the case. Choice (A) helps explain why the program is needed but the conclusion would stand even if some tenants could afford lawyers. Choice (C) concerns a possible side effect on rents, while the conclusion is only about evictions.

text: A city's library system installed self-service kiosks that let patrons borrow and return books without help from staff. In the year after installation, the number of books borrowed rose by 12 percent. The library director argues that the kiosks, by shortening waiting times at the desk, encouraged people to borrow more, and recommends installing kiosks in the system's remaining branches, which currently have none.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's argument?
options: Staff at the branches with kiosks now spend more of their time helping patrons find books and use the library's computers, rather than checking books in and out.
Kiosks require periodic software updates, during which patrons must again borrow books at the staffed desk.
At the branches with kiosks, borrowing rose most sharply among patrons who had previously borrowed only a few books each year and who had often complained about queues at the desk.
Some patrons, especially older ones, still prefer to borrow books at the staffed desk even where kiosks are available.
The number of books borrowed rose by a similar percentage at the library systems of several nearby cities during the same year.
explanation: If borrowing rose by about the same amount in nearby systems without any change to their checkout methods, a wider trend probably accounts for the rise, and the kiosks need not have caused it. Choice (C) is relevant but, if anything, fits the director's story, since the patrons who disliked queues are the ones who borrowed more. Choice (D) shows only that some patrons do not use kiosks, which is compatible with kiosks raising borrowing overall.

text: Engineers at a battery manufacturer have found that lithium cells charged at room temperature and then stored for a year lose about 8 percent of their capacity, whereas identical cells charged in a cold room lose about 15 percent. The engineers hypothesize that charging in the cold causes a thin layer of lithium metal to form on the cell's electrode, and that this layer, rather than the cold itself, is what permanently reduces capacity.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the engineers' hypothesis?
options: Cells that are stored, rather than charged, in a cold room lose capacity more slowly than cells stored at room temperature, a finding that the company has used in its advice to customers.
Lithium metal layers have been observed on electrodes of cells that were charged very rapidly at room temperature.
Cells charged slowly in the cold, a method known to prevent lithium metal from forming, lose no more capacity over a year than cells charged at room temperature.
Customers in cold climates report shorter battery life than customers in warm climates.
The company's newest cells use an electrode material that is less sensitive to temperature than the material used in older cells.
explanation: The hypothesis separates two candidate causes: the cold and the lithium layer. If cells charged in the cold without forming the layer lose no extra capacity, the cold alone does no harm and the layer is implicated, which is exactly what the engineers claim. Choice (B) shows the layer can form in other conditions but not that it reduces capacity. Choice (A) concerns storage temperature, not charging, and (D) does not distinguish the layer from the cold.

text: Analysts predicted that Quillon's decision to sell its budget smartphones only online would hurt its sales, since many budget buyers like to handle a phone in a store before buying. ⟦In the first year, Quillon's budget-phone sales did fall by 6 percent.⟧ But this figure is misleading. The entire budget-phone market shrank by 14 percent that year, so Quillon's share of the market actually grew. ⟦The online-only strategy, far from hurting Quillon, appears to have helped it,⟧ largely by allowing the company to cut prices with the money it saved on store displays.

stem: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is a finding that seems to confirm the analysts' prediction; the second is the argument's main conclusion, which opposes that prediction.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its main conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
The first is the analysts' prediction; the second is a finding that the argument offers against that prediction.
The first is a finding that the argument rejects as false; the second is a position that the argument attributes to the analysts and then criticizes as unsupported.
The first is a finding that the argument accepts as accurate but irrelevant; the second is a consideration offered in support of the argument's main conclusion about pricing.
explanation: The first portion, the 6 percent fall, appears to bear out the analysts' prediction, and the argument says it is misleading in context. The second portion is the conclusion the argument reaches using the market data: the strategy helped, not hurt. Choice (B) is wrong because the fall in sales is not evidence for that conclusion; the argument has to explain it away. Choice (E) misreads the second portion, which is the conclusion itself, while the price cuts are offered as its explanation.

text: Hospitals in the region of Aldmoor introduced a new screening program that identifies patients at high risk of developing sepsis, a dangerous response to infection, so that they can be treated early. Since the program began, the number of patients in Aldmoor's hospitals recorded as having sepsis has risen by 40 percent, yet the number of deaths from sepsis has fallen slightly.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the facts described above?
options: Sepsis is more common among elderly patients, and the share of Aldmoor's hospital patients who are over seventy has grown slowly but steadily over the past decade as the region's population has aged.
The screening program has led doctors to diagnose many mild cases of sepsis that previously would have gone unrecorded, and such cases rarely end in death.
Several hospitals outside Aldmoor that did not adopt the program have also seen a slight fall in deaths from sepsis.
Treating sepsis early requires powerful antibiotics, which can cause side effects in some patients.
Before the program began, Aldmoor's hospitals had a higher rate of deaths from sepsis than the national average.
explanation: Recorded cases rose sharply while deaths fell. If screening uncovers many mild cases that were previously missed, the count of cases grows even if no more people actually develop sepsis, and since such cases rarely kill, deaths need not rise; earlier treatment can then reduce them. Choice (A) explains a slow rise in true cases at most, not a 40 percent jump alongside falling deaths. Choice (C) suggests some other cause of fewer deaths, but it leaves the rise in recorded cases unexplained.

text: In a new study of industrial life, a historian argues that the nineteenth-century textile workers of Lowenfeld were generally content with their working conditions. As evidence, she points out that the archive of the city's largest mill contains hundreds of letters written by workers to the mill's owners, and that the great majority of these letters express gratitude for the owners' generosity, while only a handful contain complaints about wages, hours, or the conditions in the workrooms.

stem: The historian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
options: assumes without justification that the city's largest mill employed more workers than any other mill in Lowenfeld during the nineteenth century
relies on letters written in the nineteenth century, when standards of politeness in correspondence were very different from today's standards, particularly in letters between workers and employers
fails to consider that some workers may have been unable to write letters at all
overlooks the possibility that workers had reason not to complain in writing to their employers, and that the owners chose which letters to keep
takes for granted that working conditions in Lowenfeld were similar to working conditions in the textile mills of other European cities
explanation: The letters were written to the owners and kept in the owners' archive. Workers addressing their employers had strong reasons to sound grateful, and owners could have discarded unflattering letters, so the sample is likely biased toward praise. Choice (C) is tempting because it also raises representativeness, but illiteracy alone gives no reason to think nonwriters were less content; the problem is the direction of the bias, which (D) identifies. Choice (B) is vague: different politeness norms do not show that the expressed gratitude was false.

text: A university study of 400 psychology experiments published over the past fifteen years in leading journals found that those whose data were shared publicly were much less likely than others to contain statistical errors. The study's authors conclude that the expectation of outside scrutiny leads researchers to check their analyses more carefully, and they argue that journals should require all authors to share their data.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the authors' conclusion?
options: Sharing data publicly can take researchers a considerable amount of time, especially for large studies with many variables, and this burden may discourage some from submitting to journals that require it.
Some journals already require authors to share their data, while others merely encourage it.
Researchers who choose to share their data tend to be those who already check their analyses carefully, and they were just as careful in earlier work they did not share.
Some statistical errors in published experiments are discovered only years after publication, when other researchers attempt to repeat the experiments.
Most of the experiments in the study were conducted at universities in North America and Europe.
explanation: The authors claim that expected scrutiny causes more careful checking. If careful researchers are the ones who choose to share, and they were equally careful when not sharing, the lower error rate reflects who shares rather than any effect of sharing. Choice (D) is tempting, since it suggests errors in some studies were not yet found, but it applies to shared and unshared studies alike unless we assume otherwise. Choice (A) raises a cost of the recommendation without touching the causal claim.

text: Nutrition researchers measured how much vitamin D a group of volunteers absorbed from a supplement taken either with a high-fat breakfast or with a low-fat breakfast. Absorption was about 30 percent higher with the high-fat meal. The researchers conclude that people who take vitamin D supplements in order to maintain healthy blood levels of the vitamin should take them with their highest-fat meal of the day.

stem: The researchers' conclusion relies on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most people who take vitamin D supplements eat at least one high-fat meal each day.
Vitamin D is also obtained from exposure to sunlight, which varies greatly with the season.
High-fat meals have health risks that outweigh any benefit from improved absorption of vitamin D, at least for people who already eat a diet high in fat.
The volunteers in the study ate breakfasts typical of the diets of people who take vitamin D supplements.
The greater absorption seen with high-fat breakfasts would also occur when the supplement is taken with a high-fat meal at other times of the day.
explanation: The study tested only breakfasts, but the advice concerns whichever meal of the day is highest in fat. The researchers therefore assume that fat increases absorption at other meals as well, not only in the morning. Choice (A) is tempting, but the advice works even for people whose fattiest meal is modest; it says only to use the highest-fat one. Choice (C) would undercut the advice if true, so the argument certainly does not assume it, and (D) is not required because the conclusion depends on the fat content, not on the breakfasts being typical.

text: A national chain of coffee shops tested a loyalty app, which awards points toward free drinks, in twenty of its shops. Over six months, customers in those shops who used the app visited 35 percent more often than customers who did not. The chain's executives concluded that the app increases how often customers visit and decided to introduce it in all of the chain's shops.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the executives' conclusion?
options: The chain's competitors have begun to offer loyalty apps of their own, some of which give larger discounts.
During the trial, the app was promoted mainly by staff to customers they already recognized as regulars, and these customers had visited about as often before the trial began.
Customers who used the app spent slightly less per visit, on average, than customers who did not.
The twenty shops in the test were chosen to represent the full range of locations in which the chain operates, from city centers to suburban shopping malls.

Some customers who downloaded the app during the trial stopped using it after a few weeks because they found it confusing to redeem rewards, and they returned to paying in the usual way for the rest of the trial.
explanation: The executives treat the higher visit rate of app users as an effect of the app. If the users were mostly regulars who already visited that often before the trial, the difference reflects who adopted the app, not any change it caused. Choice (C) concerns spending per visit, which is relevant to whether the app pays off but not to whether it increases visits. Choice (D) actually supports the generalization from the test shops to the whole chain.

text: At Velsen University, a student qualifies for the national merit scholarship only if his or her grades are in the top tenth of the class. Every student who holds the merit scholarship is also eligible for a guaranteed room in the university's new residence hall. Last year, some students who were eligible for a guaranteed room did not receive one, although every eligible student who applied for a room by the deadline received one.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Every student at Velsen whose grades were in the top tenth of the class applied for a room last year.
Some students at Velsen who qualified for the merit scholarship did not receive the scholarship last year.
Most students who received a guaranteed room in the new residence hall last year held the merit scholarship.
Some students who were eligible for a guaranteed room did not apply for one by the deadline last year.
Only students whose grades are in the top tenth of the class are eligible for a guaranteed room.
explanation: Some eligible students did not receive a room, yet every eligible student who applied by the deadline did receive one. So those who went without cannot have applied by the deadline. Choice (E) is the trap: the passage says holding the scholarship is sufficient for eligibility, not that it is the only route, so other students might be eligible too. Choice (B) confuses receiving a room with receiving the scholarship, about which the passage says nothing.

text: A team of zoologists hypothesizes that the bright tail stripes of a species of forest frog serve to warn predators that the frog's skin is toxic. Critics suggest that the stripes might instead help males attract mates, since in many frog species bright markings play that role. The zoologists point out that in this species, females' stripes are just as bright as males' stripes.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the zoologists' hypothesis over the critics' alternative?
options: Young frogs of both sexes, which are too immature to breed, have the bright stripes and are toxic, and birds that once tasted one avoid striped frogs afterward.
In several related species, males with brighter markings are chosen more often by females during the breeding season.

The skin of this frog contains a toxin that is chemically similar to the toxins found in several other species of frog that live in the same forest, and the toxin is strong enough to sicken a snake or bird that swallows the frog.
The bright stripes of this frog become slightly duller when the frog is kept in captivity for long periods.
Some predators of this frog hunt mainly at night, when the frog's stripes are difficult to see even at close range.
explanation: If the stripes served only in courtship, frogs too young to breed would gain nothing from them. Finding the stripes on toxic juveniles, together with evidence that predators learn to avoid striped frogs, fits the warning role and is hard to explain on the mate-attraction view. Choice (C) confirms that the frog is toxic, which both sides could accept, but it does not link the stripes to that toxicity. Choice (B) supports the critics, and (E) weakens the warning hypothesis.

text: Records from the port of Tremona show that in the decade after the city's harbor was deepened in 1702, allowing much larger ships to dock, the total weight of goods passing through the port nearly doubled. Over the same decade, however, the number of dockworkers employed at the port fell by about a fifth, even though the port's handling methods, which relied entirely on manual labor, did not change.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: Shipowners began building larger ships after the harbor was deepened, because larger ships could carry more cargo at a lower cost per ton.

Many dockworkers left Tremona during the decade to work in the city's growing shipbuilding yards, which paid higher wages and offered steadier work throughout the year than loading and unloading ships did.
Before the harbor was deepened, large ships had to anchor offshore while their cargo was rowed to the docks in small boats, which required many extra workers to load and unload each cargo twice.
The goods passing through Tremona after 1702 were, on average, heavier per crate than the goods that had passed through it earlier.
Several neighboring ports were deepened during the same decade and experienced similar increases in the weight of goods handled.
explanation: With trade doubling and methods unchanged, one would expect more workers, not fewer. If large ships formerly had to unload offshore, every cargo was handled twice, by boatmen and by dockworkers; deepening the harbor removed that extra step, so much more cargo could move with less labor. Choice (B) is the attractive trap: it explains why workers left, but with handling still entirely manual it leaves unexplained how the port handled twice the goods with fewer of them. Choice (D) helps only a little, since heavier crates still require handling, and (A) explains the rise in trade, not the fall in jobs.

text: Five years ago the state of Dravia began paying a cash bonus to teachers who agreed to work in rural schools that had struggled to fill vacancies. Since then, the number of unfilled teaching positions in those schools has fallen by half. State officials argue that the bonus has solved the rural staffing problem and that the program can be ended next year without causing vacancies to rise again.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' argument?
options: Most of the teachers who took rural positions under the program are bound by contracts that require them to stay only as long as they continue to receive the bonus.
The number of unfilled teaching positions in Dravia's urban schools has also fallen over the past five years, though less sharply than in its rural schools.
Some of the rural schools in the program have also received new funding for building repairs and classroom equipment during the past five years.

The program has cost the state considerably more than officials originally estimated, largely because more teachers applied for the bonus than expected, and the legislature has asked for a full review of its spending.
Teachers in rural schools in neighboring states, which offer no bonus, earn salaries similar to those of teachers in Dravia's rural schools.
explanation: The officials grant that the bonus filled the posts but claim the gains will last after it ends. If most recruits are obliged to stay only while the bonus is paid, many may leave once it stops, and vacancies would return. Choice (C) is the attractive trap: it offers another possible cause of the improvement, but the officials' prediction is about what happens when the bonus ends, and (C) does not suggest vacancies will rise then. Choice (D) concerns cost, not staffing.

text: A company that makes wireless home security cameras, which most customers mount outdoors, plans to replace the cameras' rechargeable batteries with small solar panels. The company's engineers argue that the change will reduce customer complaints, most of which concern batteries that run down and must be recharged, and that it will not increase the number of camera failures, because the solar panels proved highly reliable in testing.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful to establish in evaluating the engineers' argument?
options: Whether the company's competitors have received a similar number of complaints about their cameras' batteries
Whether customers who complain about batteries are more likely than other customers to buy a second camera from the company
Whether the solar panels would add to the price that customers pay for each camera
Whether the cameras' other components, such as lenses and wireless transmitters, are as reliable in outdoor use as the solar panels proved to be in the company's tests
Whether the solar panels were tested in positions like those in which customers usually mount the cameras, such as under eaves and in shaded doorways
explanation: The engineers rely on test results to predict that the panels will work well in the field. If the panels were tested in full sun but customers mount cameras in shade, the panels might fail to keep cameras powered, causing both failures and complaints. Choice (D) is relevant to reliability in general, but those components are unchanged by the plan, so their reliability cannot make the switch increase failures. Choice (C) concerns price, which the argument does not address.

text: Scholars once believed that the ancient city of Kesh was abandoned suddenly, perhaps after an invasion. Recent excavations, however, found that the houses of Kesh contained almost no valuable objects such as tools, jewelry, or cooking pots, although such objects are plentiful in the city's rubbish heaps from earlier periods. The excavators conclude that the residents left gradually, taking their possessions with them, rather than fleeing in haste.

stem: The excavators' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The houses of Kesh were built of materials that would have survived for many centuries after the city was abandoned.
Kesh was not the only city in its region whose residents eventually left it.
The valuable objects missing from the houses were not removed by looters or invaders after the residents had gone.
Residents of Kesh did not throw valuable objects onto rubbish heaps, except when the objects were broken or worn out.
No other ancient city in the region was invaded during the period when Kesh was abandoned.
explanation: The excavators infer from empty houses that the residents took their things with them. That inference fails if someone else, such as invaders or later scavengers, stripped the houses after a sudden flight, so the argument must assume this did not happen. Choice (D) is tempting because it touches the rubbish-heap evidence, but that evidence only shows such objects were common earlier; the conclusion does not depend on why they were discarded. Choice (A) is not needed, since the objects, not the buildings, are the evidence.

text: A popular view holds that adults need less sleep as they age. ⟦Surveys consistently find that people over sixty-five sleep, on average, about an hour less each night than middle-aged adults do.⟧ Yet older adults also report far more daytime drowsiness and are more likely to nap. This pattern suggests that they are not choosing less sleep because they need less, but are unable to get the sleep they need. ⟦Older adults, in other words, may need just as much sleep as younger ones,⟧ and the problem worth addressing is the disruption of their sleep.

stem: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its main conclusion; the second is a position that the argument rejects.
The first is evidence that has been taken to support a view the argument opposes; the second is a conclusion the argument draws in opposition to that view.
The first is a claim that the argument disputes; the second is evidence offered in support of that claim.
The first is a finding that the argument says is mistaken; the second is the explanation the argument offers for why that finding is mistaken.

The first is a consideration offered in support of the popular view; the second is a qualification that the argument adds to that popular view in light of the evidence about naps and daytime drowsiness.
explanation: The survey finding that older adults sleep less is the natural basis for the popular view that they need less sleep. The argument accepts the finding but reinterprets it, and the second portion is its conclusion that older adults may need as much sleep as anyone, contrary to the popular view. Choice (D) is the trap: the argument never says the survey finding is mistaken, only that the inference drawn from it is. Choice (E) fails because the second portion rejects the popular view rather than qualifying it.

text: Torvald Bikes, which sells bicycles through independent shops, has seen its share of the market fall for three straight years. Its chief executive attributes the decline to the company's failure to offer electric bicycles, which now make up a quarter of all bicycle sales. Some board members argue instead that the problem is poor service at the independent shops, which customers increasingly complain about.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the chief executive's explanation rather than the board members' explanation?
options: Many independent bicycle shops have begun offering repair services for electric bicycles as well as conventional ones.
Customers who complain about service at independent bicycle shops most often mention long waits for repairs rather than problems at the time of purchase.
Electric bicycles generally earn retailers a higher profit per sale than conventional bicycles do.
Over the three years, Torvald's sales of conventional bicycles have held steady, while sales of conventional bicycles across the market have also been flat.
Torvald's main competitors, which do sell electric bicycles, also sell most of their products through independent shops.
explanation: If Torvald has kept pace in conventional bikes, where the market is flat, its share loss must come from the growing segment it does not serve: electric bikes. Poor service would presumably hurt conventional sales too, so steady conventional sales count against the board members. Choice (B) is relevant to the service complaints, but knowing what customers complain about does not show whether those complaints cost Torvald sales. Choice (E) shows competitors use the same kind of shops, which helps a little, but it says nothing about whether their service is as poor.

text: In a mountain lake, the population of a small fish species that feeds on insect larvae fell sharply after anglers illegally introduced a larger predatory fish. Biologists then removed nearly all of the predators. Over the next four years, however, the small fish recovered only slightly, even though the lake's water quality and temperature remained much as they had been before the predators arrived, and no new predators or diseases were detected.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the slow recovery of the small fish?
options: The predatory fish had fed on a wide variety of prey, including frogs and other fish species, and not only on the small fish.
Before the predators were introduced, the small fish had been one of the most abundant fish species in the lake.
Anglers who visit the lake have been informed that introducing fish is illegal and can harm the lake's native species, and a sign explaining this has been posted at the trailhead.
Small fish species in other mountain lakes have recovered rapidly after predators were removed.
While the predators were present, a species of beetle that also feeds on insect larvae multiplied greatly, and it now consumes most of the larvae on which the small fish depend.
explanation: With predators gone and conditions unchanged, quick recovery would be expected unless something else now limits the small fish. A competing beetle that grew numerous during the small fish's decline and now eats most of their food supply would hold the population down. Choice (D) makes the slow recovery more puzzling rather than explaining it. Choice (A) is relevant to the predator's effects on the lake, but it does not explain why the small fish stay scarce now that the predator is gone.

text: Researchers compared hospital records from two neighboring regions. In Region A, where a public campaign urged people with chest pain to call an ambulance at once, the death rate among heart-attack patients admitted to hospital was 9 percent. In Region B, which had no such campaign, it was 6 percent. A commentator concludes that the campaign has done more harm than good, perhaps by causing hospitals to be overcrowded with false alarms.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the commentator's conclusion?
options: Most of the people who called an ambulance in Region A because of chest pain turned out not to be having a heart attack.
Hospitals in Region A have more cardiologists per patient than hospitals in Region B, and they also have shorter average waiting times in their emergency departments.
In Region B, many heart-attack patients who would have survived only with rapid treatment died before reaching a hospital, and so were never counted among admitted patients.
The campaign in Region A was paid for by a charitable foundation rather than by the regional government.
Heart-attack death rates in both regions have fallen gradually over the past twenty years as treatments have improved and fewer people smoke.
explanation: The comparison covers only patients admitted to hospital. If, without the campaign, the most critical patients in Region B died before admission, Region B's hospital death rate looks lower simply because its sickest patients were never counted, while Region A's campaign brought such patients in alive. Choice (A) is the attractive trap: it shows the false alarms the commentator mentions really occur, which if anything supports the commentator's suggested mechanism. Choice (B) deepens the puzzle of Region A's higher rate rather than explaining it away.

text: At Hallam Consulting, every employee who leads a client project has completed the firm's management course. Some employees who have completed the management course have also earned the firm's advanced analytics certificate. No employee who has been with the firm for less than two years is permitted to enroll in the management course. Priyanka Rao joined Hallam fourteen months ago as a senior analyst in its London office.

stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Priyanka Rao does not lead a client project at Hallam.
Priyanka Rao has not earned the advanced analytics certificate.
Some employees who lead client projects at Hallam have earned the advanced analytics certificate.
Every employee at Hallam who has been with the firm for more than two years has completed the management course.
Priyanka Rao will be permitted to enroll in the management course within the next year.
explanation: Rao has been at the firm for less than two years, so she cannot have enrolled in, and thus completed, the management course; and every project leader has completed it, so she cannot lead a project. Choice (B) is the trap: nothing says the analytics certificate requires the management course, so she might hold it. Choice (C) does not follow, because the employees with the certificate need not be project leaders, and (E) assumes she will be eligible and will seek to enroll, which the statements do not establish.

text: A city transit agency plans to replace paper tickets with a smartphone app on which riders can buy fares. The agency argues that the change will cut fare evasion, because inspectors checking app tickets can instantly confirm that a ticket is valid, whereas paper tickets can be forged. The agency also expects to save money by no longer printing and distributing paper tickets.

stem: The agency's argument that the change will cut fare evasion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most of the agency's riders already own smartphones on which they could install the app.
The savings from no longer printing paper tickets will exceed the cost of developing and maintaining the app.
Inspectors currently check a smaller share of riders than they would be able to check if all tickets were on the app.
Forged paper tickets account for a meaningful share of fare evasion, rather than evasion consisting almost entirely of riders who have no ticket at all.
Riders who buy fares on the app will be less likely than other riders to lose their tickets or to forget to bring them, since few people leave home without their phones.
explanation: The agency's mechanism is that app tickets cannot be forged. That cuts evasion only if forgery is a real part of the problem; if evaders simply ride without any ticket, an unforgeable ticket changes nothing. Choice (A) matters for whether the plan is practical, but the claim about evasion could hold among app users even if some riders keep using other options. Choice (B) concerns the separate claim about saving money, and (C) is not required because the argument depends on faster verification, not on checking more riders.

text: To reduce flooding in low-lying neighborhoods, the city of Breckford plans to require that new buildings include rooftop gardens, which absorb rainwater that would otherwise run into storm drains. Critics argue that the plan will do little, because new buildings each year make up only a tiny fraction of the city's rooftops. Planners reply that the plan will be effective because most of the city's new construction is concentrated in the small area of hillside neighborhoods that drain directly into the low-lying districts.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' reply to the critics?
options: Rooftop gardens also reduce the amount of energy that buildings use for cooling during the summer.
Studies of past floods show that most of the storm water that overwhelms drains in the low-lying districts comes from the hillside neighborhoods during brief, intense rainfalls.
Rooftop gardens add considerably to the cost of constructing a new building, and developers have lobbied against the requirement.

Several other cities have adopted similar requirements for new buildings in recent years, and planners in those cities describe the programs as popular, although none has yet published data on their effects.
The low-lying neighborhoods have flooded more often in the past decade than in any earlier decade for which records exist.
explanation: The planners concede that new buildings are few but argue that their location matters. Evidence that the flood water mostly comes from the hillside neighborhoods, where the gardens would be built, shows that even a few roofs there could cut a large share of the problem. Choice (E) confirms that flooding is worsening but gives no reason to think the gardens would help. Choice (D) is weak, since no results from the other cities are available.

text: Many technology analysts argue that companies should move their computing work from their own servers to rented cloud services, since cloud providers can run servers more cheaply. ⟦For firms whose computing needs rise and fall unpredictably, this advice is sound.⟧ But for a firm whose computing load is large and steady, renting can cost more over time than owning, because the firm pays continuously for capacity it would otherwise have bought once. ⟦Such a firm, then, should keep its core work on its own servers and rent cloud capacity only to handle occasional peaks.⟧

stem: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is a consideration that has been offered against that conclusion.
The first is a position that the argument rejects; the second is a conclusion that the argument draws in opposition to that position.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support the analysts' view; the second is that view.
The first is a judgment the argument accepts within a limited scope; the second is the argument's conclusion about cases outside that scope.
The first is a prediction that the argument says has been confirmed; the second is a recommendation that the argument says follows from that prediction.
explanation: The argument endorses the analysts' advice, but only for firms with unpredictable needs; that is the first portion. It then reasons about firms with steady loads, which lie outside that scope, and concludes in the second portion that such firms should mostly own their servers. Choice (B) is the trap: the argument does not reject the analysts' advice, it limits it. Choice (A) fails because the first portion is not the main conclusion, which concerns steady-load firms.

text: A historian argues that the decline of the guilds in the city of Tolven during the 1700s was caused by the arrival of large workshops that employed unskilled laborers. As evidence, she notes that the number of guild members in Tolven fell by half between 1740 and 1780, the same period in which the number of large workshops in the city tripled, and that the guilds repeatedly petitioned the city council to restrict such workshops.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?
options: Some guild members in Tolven left their guilds to become owners or managers of the large workshops, and several of these former members later signed the petitions against further workshops.
Guild membership began to fall sharply around 1730, after the guilds steeply raised their entry fees, and most of the large workshops opened only after 1760.
Guild records from Tolven are incomplete for several years in the 1760s because a fire destroyed part of the guild hall.
Guilds in several other cities also petitioned their governments to restrict large workshops during the 1700s.
The large workshops in Tolven generally produced cheaper goods than guild members did, though the goods were of lower quality.
explanation: The historian rests her causal claim on the overlap between the workshops' rise and the guilds' decline. If the decline started earlier, after a steep rise in entry fees, and was well under way before most workshops opened, the timing points to another cause. Choice (A) is the attractive trap: members moving to the workshops actually fits the historian's view that the workshops drew people away. Choice (E) explains how workshops could compete, which supports her, and (D) is irrelevant to the cause in Tolven.

text: The country of Elbria offers a tax deduction to families who save for their children's university education in special accounts. A government report found that, since the deduction began, the total amount held in such accounts has tripled. Yet the share of Elbrian families who save anything at all for their children's education is no higher now than it was before the deduction was introduced.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?
options: Most of the money now in the special accounts was moved there from other savings by families who were already saving for education.
The cost of a university education in Elbria has risen considerably faster than the general rate of inflation since the deduction was introduced.
Families who save in the special accounts must use the money for education or else pay a penalty when they withdraw it.
Surveys show that many Elbrian families do not know that the tax deduction exists or how to open one of the special accounts at their bank.

In recent years Elbrian banks have heavily advertised the special accounts, often offering small cash bonuses to customers who open one, and the number of banks offering the accounts has doubled since the deduction began.
explanation: Account balances tripled, yet no more families save. If the growth came mainly from families who were already saving and simply shifted money into the tax-favored accounts, balances could soar without any new families beginning to save. Choice (D) is tempting because it explains why few new families joined, but it does not explain where the large increase in balances came from. Choice (E) makes the puzzle harder, since heavy advertising would be expected to draw in new savers.

text: A large employer introduced a program offering free sessions with a counselor to employees who report high levels of work stress. Among employees who used the program, the number of sick days taken fell by an average of four per year compared with the year before. The employer's human resources director argues that the program pays for itself, since the wages saved through fewer sick days exceed what the counseling costs.

stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the director's argument?
options: Whether the counselors who work in the program have training in treating workplace stress specifically
Whether employees who used the program reported greater satisfaction with their jobs afterward
Whether employees' sick days typically decline after an unusually bad year even without any intervention, and whether many joined the program just after such a year
Whether other large employers in the same industry offer similar counseling programs, and whether those programs have reduced the number of sick days their employees take
Whether employees who did not use the program took more sick days, on average, than employees who did
explanation: The director compares participants with their own previous year. If people tended to join right after an unusually stressful year with many sick days, their sick days would likely fall afterward anyway, so the savings could be overstated. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: comparing users with non-users sounds rigorous, but the groups may differ for many reasons, and the argument's comparison is with the same employees' past. Choice (B) concerns satisfaction rather than the cost savings at issue.

text: A study of grant applications to a national science foundation found that proposals reviewed by panels whose members did not know the applicants' names received higher scores, on average, when submitted by researchers at less prestigious universities than proposals from such researchers received from panels that knew the applicants' names. The study's authors conclude that when reviewers know who the applicants are, they tend to favor researchers from prestigious institutions.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the authors' conclusion?
options: Researchers at prestigious universities submit a larger number of grant proposals each year than researchers at less prestigious universities do.
Reviewers on panels that knew applicants' names reported that they tried to judge each proposal only on its scientific merit.
Proposals from researchers at less prestigious universities are, on average, shorter than proposals from researchers at more prestigious institutions.
Some reviewers on the blind panels said afterward that they could often guess which university a proposal came from by its writing style, its equipment, or the work it cited.
The proposals were assigned to blind or named panels at random, and proposals from prestigious universities received similar scores from both kinds of panel.
explanation: Random assignment means the two sets of proposals from less prestigious universities should be similar in quality, so the score gap points to the effect of knowing names. And if prestigious applicants scored the same either way, the difference arises specifically for less prestigious ones, fitting the claim of favoritism. Choice (D) is the attractive trap: guessing would make the blind panels less blind, which works against finding any difference, so if anything it suggests the true effect is understated, but it adds no evidence that the gap reflects favoritism. Choice (B) is a self-report that cannot rule out unconscious bias.

text: Pellam Airlines began charging passengers a fee for each checked bag two years ago. Since then, the average time its planes spend at the gate between flights has fallen by eight minutes, allowing the airline to schedule more flights each day. Pellam's managers conclude that the fee, by encouraging passengers to bring fewer bags, has shortened loading times, and they plan to raise the fee further to shorten turnaround times still more.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' plan to shorten turnaround times by raising the fee?
options: Several of Pellam's competitors introduced checked-bag fees during the same two years, and their turnaround times also fell, by amounts similar to Pellam's, over the same period of time.
Since the fee was introduced, Pellam's revenue from checked-bag fees has exceeded the airline's original estimates.
Since the fee began, far more passengers carry bags into the cabin, and boarding is now held up chiefly by passengers searching for overhead space, a delay that a higher checked-bag fee would worsen.
Some passengers have switched from Pellam to rival airlines that do not charge for checked bags, especially on long-distance routes where most travelers carry more luggage.
Two years ago Pellam also began using larger baggage carts that allow ground crews to load and unload the hold faster than before, even when planes carry a full load of checked bags.
explanation: The plan assumes that a higher fee will keep shortening turnarounds. If the bottleneck is now cabin boarding slowed by carry-on bags, a higher fee would push still more bags into the cabin and lengthen turnaround times. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: it offers another cause of the past improvement and so weakens the claim about the fee's effect, but it does not show that raising the fee would fail. Choice (A) suggests the fee works similarly elsewhere, which fits the managers' view.

text: Astronomers have found that stars in a certain cluster that host large, close-orbiting planets rotate, on average, faster than otherwise similar stars in the cluster that have no such planets.
